about.heading: About
body: I'm a Unity developer and creative technologist from Medellín, Colombia. I study Digital Entertainment Design Engineering at Universidad Pontificia Bolivariana (UPB) and I'm finishing the Junior Unity Developer bootcamp at Generation Colombia.

What I enjoy most is the moment an idea starts to respond: a jump that finally feels right, an AR filter that follows your hands, a room in VR you can reach into. I co-founded BioFrame, an early-stage creative technology studio, where I prototype interactive solutions, and in 2026 I helped other students build their VR and AR projects as a teaching assistant at UPB.

My personal brand, the Navigator, comes from how I work: I plan with structure, and when the plan breaks I recalculate instead of stopping. The logo is a delta wing shaped like a boomerang, a nod to my first dream of flying and to a path that keeps moving forward even when it has to turn back. The moving field at the top of this page is that idea in code.

I use AI tools, mainly Claude, as a tutor, a pair programmer and a testing assistant. They help me learn faster and ship sooner, but I don't keep code I can't explain. Each project page says what the AI did and what I did.
I'm looking for my first role in the industry, as a junior Unity developer, in XR, or in QA. Testing a build, measuring it and writing down what breaks is part of how I work.

mohan.title: El Silbido del Mohán
mohan.subtitle: The Mohán's Whistle
mohan.pitch: A 2D platformer where you jump between the real world and the spirit world to gather offerings for the Mohán, a river spirit from Colombian folklore, and escape before it catches you.
mohan.role: Gameplay programmer: I built every mechanic in the game
mohan.context: Made for Game Jam #2 of Generation Colombia's Junior Unity Developer bootcamp, on the theme "Two Worlds". My teammates handled art, UI art, sound and documentation, and I wrote all the gameplay code.
did: Player controller with movement, jump, faster falling, coyote time and jump buffering.
World switching on one key, through a WorldManager singleton that sends events so every other system reacts on its own. It refuses to switch when the player would end up inside solid ground.
Objects that exist only in the real world, only in the spirit world, or in both.
The offering pickups, the altar that counts them, the escape sequence with its exit portal, and the game over screen.
The Mohán meter, the tension bar that fills while you stay in the spirit world.
Every value that a designer might tune, such as distances, timings, speeds and texts, exposed in the Inspector so the team could adjust the game without touching code.

challenges.title: Making the jump feel good
challenges.body: The first jump felt floaty and missed inputs near ledges. I doubled gravity on the way down, capped the fall speed, and added 0.1 s of coyote time and jump buffering. I also set the jump height in tiles with a gizmo in the editor, so level design and physics speak the same units.

challenges.title: Getting the browser build ready for itch.io
challenges.body: Before publishing, I ran a QA pass on the WebGL build with an AI agent connected to the Unity Editor. We profiled memory and download size, and found the long music tracks were set to decompress on load, which could take an estimated 80 to 90 MB of memory each. I switched them to compressed in memory, changed the compression to the format itch.io serves natively and stripped unused code. The result: about 27.5 MB to download, 144 FPS at the monitor's cap and zero console errors. I wrote it all up as a checklist for the team.

gallery: Title screen of El Silbido del Mohán: pixel art of a fisherman in a yellow raincoat rowing a canoe at sunset, with ruins on the horizon.
ai: I worked with Claude as a tutor and pair programmer. It explained techniques such as coyote time and jump buffering, suggested ways to structure the systems and reviewed my code. I built the mechanics step by step with that guidance, and I know what every line does and why it's there.
For the browser build, I connected Claude to the Unity Editor as an AI agent to check project settings and profile the WebGL build. I reviewed each change before applying it.
Commits, pull requests and design decisions stayed with me and my team.

embed.size: Loads about 29 MB only after you click. Needs a keyboard.
embed.note: Works best on a computer. Controls: A and D to move, Space to jump, W to switch worlds, Esc to pause.

espejo-magico.title: Espejo Mágico
espejo-magico.subtitle: Magic Mirror for the Telemedellín tour
espejo-magico.pitch: An interactive mirror for the Telemedellín studio tour. Visitors control it with hand gestures, try on AR filters and take their photo home with a QR code.
espejo-magico.role: UX/UI, integration, computer vision and programming
espejo-magico.team: Six people: four from animation and two from interactive experiences
espejo-magico.context: Final project of Workshop 7, the course that brings together the whole Digital Entertainment Design Engineering program at UPB, with a real client: Telemedellín invited us to renew part of its museum tour. In our visits we saw that the makeup for film and TV exhibit was practically invisible: 70 to 80% of visitors walked past it, and the infographic went unread. Espejo Mágico turns it into a mirror you control with your hands, where four of the channel's presenters show how they are made up for the screen, and makeup is presented as part of the job for men and women alike. It won the program's highest recognition, voted by the faculty jury at the DEX 2026-1 awards.
did: Designed the visitor experience, from the first gesture in front of the mirror to the photo they take home.
Integrated machine learning hand tracking so visitors control the mirror without touching anything.
Trained an object recognition model with Teachable Machine so the camera identifies 3D-printed makeup tools (a lipstick, a brush and others) and starts the matching presenter's animated sequence.
3D printed those makeup tools from the models made by the animation team.
Connected Snapchat's AR API to apply the makeup filters, and Cloudinary to store each photo and deliver it through a QR code.
Built and maintained both versions of the experience, one in Unity and one for the web.

challenges.title: Recognizing objects in real lighting
challenges.body: The model confused objects when the light changed or the background wasn't uniform. We reduced the errors by retraining it with more examples and controlling the lighting around the mirror, although it never became perfect in the time we had.

challenges.title: Performance, and moving from an app to the web
challenges.body: The animations and audio made the project heavy, and the original plan of shipping a Unity APK ran into technical problems. We moved the experience to a web version and baked the audio into the renders to simplify playback. The change paid off: the browser let us build the mirror surface that ripples like mercury when you move your hand.

challenges.title: What 11 user tests changed
challenges.body: Testers loved that the mirror reacts to them without touching anything and that the printed objects trigger the content, but the pinch gesture to choose a presenter wasn't intuitive. We redesigned the gesture instructions and added Telemedellín's identity (logo, colors and references to the channel) to the interface.

gallery: Start screen of Espejo Mágico: the four animated presenters on a TV set behind a mirror frame lined with light bulbs, with the Telemedellín logo.
ai: Recognizing the makeup tools is itself an AI model, which I trained with Teachable Machine on examples of the 3D-printed objects. The background music was generated with AI, and the voice-over was recorded by UPB's voice team.

I also worked with an AI assistant as a guide while connecting the APIs (hand tracking, Snapchat's AR API and Cloudinary): it helped me understand how each integration works so I could build it and get it running myself.

embed.note: Works best on a computer with Chrome or Edge and a camera. Make a pinch gesture to move forward. Keys: N opens the presenters menu, M goes back to the mirror.

vr-apartment.title: VR Apartment
vr-apartment.subtitle: A studio apartment you can walk around and touch in VR
vr-apartment.pitch: Put on a Meta Quest headset, teleport around a furnished studio apartment, open its doors and drawers, and pick up everyday objects with your hands.
vr-apartment.role: Co-developer: we worked as a pair on every part of the project
vr-apartment.team: Pair project with María Paulina Serna Alzate. We built it together, most of the time at the same computer.
vr-apartment.context: Midterm project for the VR and AR course at UPB: take a ready-made apartment and turn it into a space you can explore and use in VR. The architecture and furniture come from a free Asset Store pack; our work was making it interactive.
did: Set up a Unity 6 (URP) project for Meta Quest with OpenXR and the Meta XR SDK, built for Android and tested on Quest 2, Quest 3S and Quest 3.
Cleaned up the apartment model: removed duplicate objects and joined loose parts, like drawers split into separate pieces, into prefabs that could become interactive.
Used Meta Interaction SDK building blocks for hand grab and touch grab, so you pick objects up with your own hands.
Made 15 everyday objects grabbable, including the TV remote, cutlery, plates, a cutting board, a lamp, a laptop, a magazine and photo frames.
Added doors that swing on their hinges when you push them and kitchen drawers that slide out, using angular and linear movement limits.
Placed teleport points around the apartment and fixed the NavMesh so teleporting lands only where you can stand.
Fitted colliders room by room (walls, bathroom, kitchen, dining room) and enabled GPU instancing to keep the headset running smoothly.

challenges.title: Making a ready-made model interactive
challenges.body: The apartment model wasn't optimized for interaction. It had duplicate objects, and things like drawers came as loose individual parts. We took the time to clean up the duplicates and join each piece into a single prefab before we could make anything interactive.

challenges.title: Physics that feels right in your hands
challenges.body: Choosing between kinematic and physics-driven objects, and getting doors to rotate naturally when you push them with your hands, took a lot of testing. Each grabbable object also needed several colliders fitted to its shape so the grab matched what you see.

challenges.title: Two people, one Unity scene
challenges.body: A Git merge conflict in the shared scene almost cost us the project. We recovered by duplicating the scene and agreeing that each of us would work on different objects, never the same ones at the same time. It taught us to plan who touches what before opening the scene.

ar-card.title: AR Business Card
ar-card.subtitle: My first steps in AR: a business card that comes alive
ar-card.pitch: Point your phone at a printed business card and a 3D version of me appears on it, waves hello and links to my profiles, with a video playing beside it.
ar-card.role: Solo developer: AR setup, interactions, 3D buttons and Android build
ar-card.context: First assignment ("Mis primeros pasos") of the VR and AR course at UPB: a marker-based AR experience in Unity with Vuforia.
did: Set up a Unity 6 (URP) project with Vuforia Engine 11 and ARCore, and created image targets for the front and the back of the card.
Created my 3D character with Ready Player Me and animated it with Mixamo. Along the way I also explored Avaturn and Blender as other ways to build and prepare the character.
Placed the avatar on the card with idle and waving animations. Tapping it triggers a run-and-flip animation.
Added 3D GitHub, LinkedIn and Instagram icons that open my profiles when tapped.
Modeled play and pause buttons in Blender to control a video that plays on the card.
Built and tested the Android app.

challenges.title: Getting the card to track steadily
challenges.body: The hardest part was making the phone recognize the card reliably. Vuforia rates each image target with stars according to how many distinct features the camera can find. Following Vuforia's documentation, I adjusted the card artwork toward more organic shapes and more corners, which give the camera more points to hold on to, and checked every version against that rating in Vuforia's Target Manager until the card tracked well on the phone.

voces.title: Voces – Objects That Speak
voces.subtitle: Talking display cases for the Juan del Corral Museum
voces.pitch: Two interactive pieces for museums in Santa Fe de Antioquia: an antique phone that lets you call people from the town's past, and display cases where the objects tell their own story while lights highlight each one.
voces.team: Team of four: project manager, head of engineering, UI/UX designer (me), and narrative and concept
voces.context: Workshop 6 (Interactive Experiences) at UPB. Our studio of 13 students proposed Memoria Viva, three connected experiences for the Juan del Corral Museum and the Museum of Religious Art in Santa Fe de Antioquia. Voces was my team's part. In a field visit on 30 August 2025 we saw that the tour relied mostly on posters and that the objects didn't create an emotional connection, so we set out to let visitors listen to the past instead of only looking at it.
did: Designed the experience and the interface of both pieces as the team's UI/UX designer.

Built the digital prototypes in p5.js: an antique phone where you dial a character from a directory and hear their story, and a display case that narrates its objects, so we could test both ideas before moving to hardware.
Built the physical display case prototype with the head of engineering: a presence sensor starts the sequence when a visitor comes within range, and LEDs light each object as the voice mentions it.
Modeled and sculpted the display case pieces in Blender (a shirt, a mask and a statue), testing shapes until they were ready for 3D printing.
Ran usability tests together with the team and turned the findings into design changes.

challenges.title: What the usability tests changed
challenges.body: Most people understood the phone right away and found it more engaging than the display cases. Some didn't know which object the case was talking about, so we changed the start: the light reaches the object before the voice begins. Testers also pointed out that a green call icon in my phone prototype felt too modern, so we removed elements that recall today's technology and made the directory more visual. The AI voices felt mysterious and interesting, but people asked for them to sound more human and closer to each character.

ai: The character voices were made with AI. Nicolás Quintero, in charge of narrative, used Pinokio and ElevenLabs to train a voice model on his own voice and gave it a different tone for each character; the woman's voice came from the ElevenLabs voice library. The scripts, the experience design, the prototypes and the hardware were made by the team. Our usability tests also measured how comfortable visitors felt listening to AI voices.

semana-santa.title: Santa Pasión
semana-santa.subtitle: A Holy Week video mapping for Santa Fe de Antioquia, simulated in Unity
semana-santa.pitch: A night-time walk through the square of the Church of Jesús Nazareno in Santa Fe de Antioquia while a narrator guides you through Lent, Holy Week and Easter, and the church facade, its altar and the houses around it light up with projected video.
semana-santa.role: Project lead, Unity developer, 3D modeler and narrative
semana-santa.context: Workshop 5 of the Interactive Experiences line at UPB. Our studio designed Sancta Lumina, a Holy Week route through three emblematic churches of Santa Fe de Antioquia (La Chinca, Jesús Nazareno and Santa Bárbara), each with its own experience. The Museum of Religious Art, part of the Archdiocese of Santa Fe de Antioquia, opened its space to us for this project. My team designed the second act, Santa Pasión, for the square and Church of Jesús Nazareno: a 15-minute sensory route in three scenes. We couldn't project on the real building, so I simulated the video mapping in Unity and presented the complete sequence.
did: Modeled the square, the surrounding houses and the church in Blender.
Wrote the narrative: three scenes (Lent, Holy Week and Easter), each led by its liturgical color (white and gold, purple, red) and guided by a narrator's voice.
Built the simulation in Unity 6 (URP), with the projected videos playing on surfaces fitted to the church facade, the altar and the houses.
Directed the whole sequence with Timeline and Cinemachine cameras, in sync with the voice-over and the soundscape.
Lit the night scene with architectural lighting and exported the Windows build we used to present it.

challenges.title: Coming back to Unity for something that wasn't a game
challenges.body: It was my first time back in Unity after a long time away, and not to make a game but to prototype an experience. Besides getting comfortable with the editor again, I had to tell a story with Timeline and Cinemachine cameras instead of handing control to a player.

challenges.title: Simulating a projection we couldn't do for real
challenges.body: The hardest part was integrating everything and making the simulation believable. I solved it by playing each video on a plane fitted to the shape of the building, so the projection follows the facade and the altar. We were left wanting to add volumetric lighting to show the projector beams in the air.

ai: The visuals projected on the buildings were generated by the team with OpenAI's Sora, from moodboards and references we prepared, to go with the narrated sequence. The 3D models, the Unity scene, the timeline and the narrative were made without AI.

design-system.title: Microsoft Teams redesign
design-system.subtitle: A design sprint to bring real-time teamwork into Microsoft Teams
design-system.pitch: Students only opened Teams when a professor required it and moved to Discord, Figma or Miro to actually work together. We redesigned Teams around a "Coworking" space where a team pins its boards and apps and starts working in real time.
design-system.role: TODO: Your role in the team
design-system.context: UX/UI course at UPB, run as a design sprint around one question: how could Teams give us tools to work in real time, as a team? Every student in our survey used Teams for school, but most rarely used it for teamwork and preferred Discord, Figma, Miro or WhatsApp. They found it unintuitive, couldn't tell what its integrations were for, and missed shared boards they could edit at the same time.
did: Ran the Understand phase: a survey and interviews, quantitative and qualitative insights, affinity clustering and "How might we" questions.
Defined the target, the design principles, a risk map and an assumptions map, and set the product's personality.

Mapped the user flows and designed the redesign: a Coworking channel with pinned boards, app groups and a one-click way to start a coworking session, plus an apps store with tutorials for each integration.
Wrote the usability test script with tasks such as pinning an app, creating a Coworking zone and finding the monthly updates, ran the tests and turned the errors into hotfixes.

gimmy.title: Gimmy
gimmy.subtitle: A gamified gym device, taken from user research to business plan
gimmy.pitch: A small device that clips magnetically onto gym machine weights, tracks every rep and connects over Bluetooth to an app that turns training into minigames, rewards and weekly challenges.
gimmy.context: Digital Entertainment Project Management (GYRPED) course at UPB. The idea came from the high dropout rate in gyms, especially among beginners: what if training worked like a game, with progression, constant feedback and rewards? Over the semester we documented the whole project in a 43-page management book, from user research to business model, financial plan, marketing and risks. The project stayed at concept stage: we didn't build the software or the electronics.
did: Managed and organized the project as the team's project manager, and wrote the 43-page management book.

Led the research: a survey of 70 people with different relationships to the gym, 18 people's opinions about the idea, competitor analysis, user archetypes, and the product description and value proposition.
Shaped the idea and the narrative of the product with the team, and outlined the electronics approach we would need to build it.
Prepared my teammates' 3D models in Blender and 3D printed every proposal with Ultimaker Cura.
Every decision went through team reviews and proposals; my core was management, organization, design and research.

challenges.title: Putting numbers on something that doesn't exist yet
challenges.body: The hardest part was projecting the costs and the budget: what the team, the components and the launch would need, all as estimates for a product nobody had built. We had to back each figure with research and accept that the plan would change once real prices came in.

challenges.title: From concept to a working device
challenges.body: Making Gimmy real would mean electronics that read each rep and send it reliably to the phone. The course didn't ask us to build it, but we got closer than required: I 3D printed every proposal so we could hold the shape in our hands. It remains a project we could try to build in the future.

ai: We used AI image generation to visualize the device from our own descriptions, so we could show what it might look like in the group presentations. The app design, the sketches, the 3D models, the research and the management book were made by the team.
gallery: Hand sketch of the device by Mateo Barón, front and back: camera sensor, Bluetooth, battery and volume buttons, USB-C port, a magnet on the back and a removable elastic band.

Gimmy app screens designed in Figma by Mateo Barón: a progress dashboard, the exercise filter, the choice between audio and minigame training, a minigame running during a bench press set, and the weekly commitment step.
The onboarding evaluation: welcome screen and questions about fitness goal, gender, age, fitness level and preferred type of exercise.
Splash screen, sign in, sign up and the start of a workout.
